results.question: You receive two Visa card offers: Option A is free but charges 1.5% on every foreign transaction. Option B costs CHF 8/month but has zero foreign fees. You travel to Europe 2–3 times a year. Which do you pick and why?
results.answer: I would likely take the CHF 8 option, but only if we actually spend enough abroad as a family. With holidays and hotels, those foreign fees add up quickly, so I want predictability. Still, I would quickly estimate our yearly travel spend to be sure the CHF 96 fee is really justified. If it is only small trips, I would stay with the free card.

results.question: Your bank sends you a message: your free debit card will be replaced by a new Visa card at CHF 5/month. You can opt out and keep a basic account. What do you do?
results.answer: I would opt out and keep the free option. CHF 5 per month is not huge, but I don't see a clear benefit for our daily family spending. My debit card already works for groceries and bills, so I don't need to pay just for a different label. I prefer to keep things simple and only pay if there is real value.

results.question: A new Visa card offers 1% cashback on all Migros and Coop purchases. The monthly fee is CHF 4. Would this change how you pay at the supermarket?
results.answer: Yes, that is actually interesting because groceries are a big part of our budget. If I clearly get more than CHF 4 back each month, then it makes sense for the family. I would probably switch to that card for supermarket shopping. But I would still keep it limited to that use and not complicate everything else.

results.question: Which of these would make you most likely to get a Visa card: (a) 2% cashback, (b) travel insurance included, (c) no foreign transaction fees, (d) a CHF 100 welcome bonus?
results.answer: For me, it is clearly the 2% cashback. That directly reduces our everyday costs, especially groceries and family expenses. The others are nice but more occasional or one-time benefits. I prefer something simple and ongoing that I can see every month.

results.question: You currently use Twint for almost everything. A Visa card promises the same speed but adds rewards. What would it take for you to actually switch?
results.answer: It would need to be very simple and clearly beneficial every month. If I have to track points or complicated rewards, I lose interest quickly. A straightforward cashback that I can see on our grocery spending would convince me. Otherwise, I prefer to stick with what already works.

results.question: Have you ever been in a situation where Twint or your debit card was not accepted? What did you do — and would a credit card have solved it?
results.answer: Yes, occasionally on holidays or some online bookings, especially abroad. In those cases, I either used a credit card or had to find another option, which is not always convenient with children waiting. A credit card definitely helps in those situations. That is one of the few cases where I see real value.

results.question: A Visa card gives you CHF 50 welcome bonus but requires CHF 6/month for 12 months — total cost CHF 72. Is that a good deal to you?
results.answer: No, that doesn't feel like a good deal. I end up paying more than I receive, so it's not really a benefit. These welcome bonuses often sound better than they are. I prefer something that gives ongoing value, not a short-term incentive.

results.question: If a Visa card saved you CHF 15/month through cashback and discounts, but cost CHF 10/month in fees, would you see that as a net gain or still feel reluctant?
results.answer: Mathematically it is a gain, but I would still double-check how realistic that CHF 15 saving is. If it comes from normal family spending like groceries, then yes, it makes sense. But if it depends on special offers or extra effort, I become skeptical. I prefer predictable savings.

results.question: What is the absolute maximum monthly fee you would accept for a Visa card — and only under what conditions?
results.answer: For me, CHF 10 is the absolute maximum, and only if the benefits clearly exceed that every month. It must be simple, like cashback on groceries or useful family expenses. I would also expect strong security and purchase protection. Otherwise, I would not pay that much.

results.question: If a Visa card were completely free forever but offered no rewards, would you still get one? What would be the point for you?
results.answer: Yes, I would still get one as a backup, especially for travel and online purchases. It is useful for situations where debit or Twint does not work. But I would not use it daily without any benefits. For everyday spending, I would stick to my usual methods.
